extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, prosecutors, KIPO officials, and other practitioners/scholars of Korean patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive chapter outlining the Republic of Korea's patent system: institutional structure (KIPO, IPTAB, Patent Court), administrative and judicial procedures (ex parte/inter partes trials, revocation suits), specialized judiciary features, criminal enforcement, and procedural rules (time limits, standing, jurisdiction, evidence scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the Patent Act (Article 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act states its purpose in Article 1 as being “to promote technical development by protecting and encouraging inventions and promoting their use in order to contribute to industrial growth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames patent law as balancing protection of inventors with public domain access; overarching theme of balancing public and private interests to promote industrial growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional protection of patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent right is a property right and is thus protected under the general provision of the Constitution guaranteeing property rights; Article 22(2) specifically sets forth that “the rights of authors, inventors, scientists, engineers and artists shall be protected by the law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent rights should be exercised proportionally to their value and in a manner that promotes justice and fairness; constitutional context informs litigation and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of IPTAB proceedings (ex parte vs inter partes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of IPTAB proceedings: ex parte (appeal against examiner’s rejection, trial for correction, patent opposition heard ex parte since March 2017) and inter partes (trial for invalidation; trial to confirm the scope of rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte involves only the petitioner; inter partes involve petitioner and defendant disputing a granted right. The list of trials falling under each category is provided to classify matters for IPTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal against decision to reject an application (IPTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant receives a decision of rejection from an examiner, they may pursue an appeal within 30 days of the date of receipt of the certified copy of the decision (Article 132-17 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 30-day appeal period is a strict procedural requirement for ex parte appeals against examiner rejections at IPTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial for correction (IPTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder may pursue a petition for the correction of a granted patent or utility model for reasons of narrowing a claim, correcting a clerical error, or clarifying an ambiguous description (Article 136 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible corrections are limited to specified grounds; correction procedure is an ex parte IPTAB remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent opposition (IPTAB) and time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may request a patent opposition, within six months of the publication of the grant of the patent, to revoke the patent based on prior art (Article 132-2 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions are time-limited (six months from grant publication) and are a post-grant mechanism to challenge novelty/prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial for invalidation (IPTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interested party may seek a trial to retroactively invalidate the granted patent right based on statutory invalidation grounds (Article 133 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidation is an inter partes procedure; grounds follow statutory invalidation provisions and may be pursued by parties with interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial to confirm the scope of rights (IPTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interested party may seek a trial to confirm whether a technology that is being practiced or will be practiced by a third party falls within the scope of a granted patent (Article 135 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine whether third-party activities fall within patent scope; inter partes format applies when rights are disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of hearings at IPTAB (written vs oral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings may be held orally or in writing. Unless requested otherwise, hearings are conducted generally in writing. An oral hearing is held upon request from the parties or if the presiding administrative judge finds it necessary (Patent Act, art. 154(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can request oral hearings; the presiding judge may order oral hearing when necessary—default is written proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPTAB panel composition and decision rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A panel of three or five administrative judges hears a case and participates in deliberations to reach a conclusion by a majority vote before rendering the final decision (Patent Act, art. 146).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are by majority; appeal from final IPTAB decision goes to the Patent Court; procedural composition affects deliberation and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non bis in idem effect of IPTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IPTAB decision on a case becomes final and conclusive, no person may demand a retrial based on the same facts or evidence; this does not apply where the final and conclusive ruling is a rejection. 'Same facts' means facts stemming from the same cause with respect to the same right; 'same evidence' includes evidence submitted before the confirmed decision as well as supplementary evidence not compelling enough to overturn it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New, compelling evidence that is sufficient to overturn a confirmed decision is not barred by non bis in idem; rejections are excepted from the finality bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between revocation suits and administrative trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Revocation suits (judicial) are adversarial and require parties to make arguments and submit materials; administrative IPTAB trials are inquisitorial. Arguments/materials presented in an IPTAB trial cannot be automatically treated as presented in a revocation suit—the court requires new presentation/submission for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should prepare to re-plead and re-submit evidence in judicial revocation suits even if they were part of the IPTAB record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction for revocation actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 186(1) of the Patent Act sets forth that the Patent Court has exclusive jurisdiction over revocation actions; normally administrative suits fall under Administrative Procedure Act but Patent Act confers exclusivity to the Patent Court for revocation suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation suits must be filed in the Patent Court as court of first instance for such matters; other administrative patent litigation categories may fall to administrative courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrated jurisdiction for civil patent cases (since 2016)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments effective Jan 1, 2016 concentrated original jurisdiction of civil patent cases to specified district courts (those where high courts are seated: Seoul Central concurrent) and enlarged the Patent Court’s exclusive appellate jurisdiction over civil appeals concerning patent and other listed IP rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-instance civil patent litigation is limited to designated district courts to avoid inconsistent outcomes; appeals go to Patent Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Court organization and special division criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court has general divisions (five, each of three judges) with random case assignment; a special division (Chief Judge + two judges) may be formed for cases that could become important precedent, significantly influence society, or lack sufficient precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases of high importance, societal impact, or novelty may be reallocated to the special division for more rigorous adjudication and research support.

rubrics_metrics.name: International divisions: handling of foreign-language and foreign-party cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A case may be handled as an international case when a party is foreign or a foreign company, material evidence is in a foreign language, or other international circumstances exist; consent of the adverse party is required and courts may refuse if significant delay expected. Permission is currently limited to English; parties may make oral arguments or file documents in the permitted foreign language without translation; decisions are rendered in Korean and translations provided after service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission must be applied in writing before the first trial date (with exceptions); effect of permission is limited to the court level; interpretation is provided at oral hearings; translations of decisions are supplied for parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized patent judges and staffing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: While there are no express statutory requirements for qualification, the Patent Court seeks judges with science/engineering/IP backgrounds, judges experienced exclusively in IP matters, or former practitioners; the court aims for longer term assignments of such judges and secures technical support staff (judicial technical examiners/researchers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization (education, background, tenure) is treated as important for consistent and knowledgeable adjudication of technical patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial education for IP judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judicial Research and Training Institute offers annual IP Litigation Training for judges handling patent cases for the first time and Advanced IP Litigation Training every two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing education, online judge communities, practice research committees, and joint courts’ seminars support expertise development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of revocation suits and principle of original dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit can only be filed against the original disposition (principle of original dispositions), except where the adjudication itself is legally flawed (principle of exceptional adjudication). The Patent Act allows suits only against adjudications on administrative appeals for revocation of IPTAB decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs must frame complaints correctly (seek revocation of IPTAB decision by date/case number) rather than seeking direct declarations like 'patent number shall become null and void'; certain administrative decisions cannot be directly sued without IPTAB procedure first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to institute a revocation suit
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit may only be instituted by a party to the IPTAB trial, an intervenor in the IPTAB trial, or a person who sought to intervene in the IPTAB trial but was denied (Patent Act, art. 154(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary third parties without IPTAB participation lack standing; plaintiffs must have been participants or attempted participants in IPTAB proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing period for revocation suits (30 days) and extension rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit must be filed within 30 days from the date when a certified copy of the relevant IPTAB decision or ruling was served. The 30-day period cannot be extended or shortened by the court; the presiding judge of the IPTAB may, ex officio, grant an additional period for persons in remote areas or with poor access—practically foreigners overseas often receive 20–30 day additional periods. An extension granted after lapse of the initial 30 days does not cure an already-lapsed initial period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict adherence to the 30-day rule is required; parties should seek any necessary IPTAB additional periods in advance and treat the initial period as sacrosanct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of examination in revocation suits (limitation vs nonlimitation theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two theories whether revocation suits are limited to grounds/evidence claimed in the IPTAB trial (limitation theory) or not (nonlimitation theory). The Supreme Court has upheld the nonlimitation theory for inter partes cases: a revocation suit examines substantive or procedural unlawfulness present at the time of the disposition and may consider unlawfulness beyond what was presented at IPTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigants may raise and courts may examine grounds beyond the IPTAB record in inter partes revocation suits; parties should be prepared to litigate broader issues on judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction principles for infringement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine patent infringement, interpretation of the scope of claims is required with focus on the language and text stated in the scope of claims (principle of literal interpretation), while also taking into account the descriptions and drawings of the invention and common technical knowledge at the time the application was filed (principle of reference to the descriptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal interpretive first; descriptions and common general knowledge used as reference; elements present only in descriptions (not claims) should not be compared against alleged infringing product/process elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element comparison requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To fall within the protective scope of a patented invention, the defendant’s product or process must include all elements of the patented invention; if only some elements are included and others missing, the product/process does not fall within the protective scope in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement requires presence of all claim elements (literal infringement) but doctrine of equivalents may apply where elements are not literally identical but are equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of literal infringement and doctrine of equivalents; indirect infringement not criminal
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent infringement includes both literal infringement and infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. Court precedent takes the position that indirect infringement is fundamentally a preparatory act and cannot be punished criminally absent a specific provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal prosecutions focus on direct (literal or equivalent) infringement; indirect/preparatory acts typically not subject to criminal sanction under existing precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required for criminal patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: For criminal patent infringement to be established, (i) a valid patent right should exist, (ii) the product or process practicing the patent right should be within the protective scope of the patent right, (iii) the alleged infringer’s practice of the patent right should be unlawful, (iv) the alleged infringer should have the ability to fulfill their legal responsibility, and (v) the alleged infringer should have intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All five elements must be considered; the second element (scope comparison) is often the most contested in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for patent invalidation in criminal cases (novelty/inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: If elements of a patented invention are identical to prior art known at the time of application and thus lack novelty, the patented invention has no scope of right worth protecting regardless of absence of an invalidation decision, and patent infringement is not established. Whether lack of inventive step can be reviewed in criminal cases is unsettled, but common view is that no criminal infringement will be found if a lack of inventive step is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may raise novelty/inventive-step defenses in criminal proceedings; courts may consider administrative/judicial invalidation progress when handling such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent in criminal patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'intent' refers to the awareness and acceptance of patent infringement; it cannot be readily concluded on the sole basis of a registered patent. The Criminal Act allows exculpation for reasonable legal mistake (art.16) but courts are strict about whether advice (e.g., from a patent attorney) constitutes reasonable ground for misunderstanding of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (e.g., warning letters) may be used to show intent; mere receipt of legal advice is unlikely alone to relieve criminal intent without convincing justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of offenses principle in criminal patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one person has committed multiple infringements, a single comprehensive offense may be established if the unity and continuity of their criminal intent is recognized; only one offense of infringement is established for each patent right regardless of multiple acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity of acts may be aggregated into one offense for sentencing if continuity/unity of intent exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory punishment for patent infringement and related criminal provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory punishment for patent infringement is imprisonment with labor for not more than seven years or a fine not exceeding KRW 100 million. Other criminal provisions address obtaining a patent by fraud (imprisonment up to three years or fine up to KRW 30 million) and breach of confidentiality orders (imprisonment up to five years or fine up to KRW 50 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal exposure varies by specific offense and aggravating factors; related statutes address fraud and confidentiality breaches in addition to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing factors in criminal patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to be considered in sentencing include whether the patented invention is actually practiced by the patentee, whether the defendant is in a competitive relationship with the patentee, whether the infringement is literal or under the doctrine of equivalents, the degree of infringement, the degree of damage inflicted on the victim, whether an agreement was reached, and the degree of intent to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical sentencing outcomes have tended toward fines and probation rather than imprisonment; courts weigh commercial context, harm, and mens rea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture and corporate/joint penal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any article created by patent infringement or obtained by such infringement can be confiscated or ordered to be delivered to the injured party upon request (Patent Act, art. 231(1)). If a representative/agent/employee commits infringement in connection with business, both offender and corporation/individual may be penalized unless the corporation/individual was not negligent in supervision (Patent Act, art. 230).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victims may seek confiscation/delivery of infringing goods; companies risk corporate penalties unless adequate supervision can be demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation/charging process and two-track investigation system
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary investigators of patent infringement are divided into general judicial police officers and special judicial police officers of the KIPO; prosecutors may conduct supplementary investigations or have cases transferred. Patent infringement is now an offense not punishable only upon complaint; special judicial police officers may recognize infringement if discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although formal powers changed, in practice many prosecutions still follow patentee complaints; focal prosecutors’ offices and specialized investigation departments have been established to handle complex technical cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent investigation advisor system
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent investigation advisors (experienced patent attorneys and KIPO officials) are appointed to provide technical advice to focal prosecutors’ offices and specialized investigation departments; advisors may be directly hired by the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office or dispatched from the KIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisors support technical assessment during investigations and prosecutions but trials occur in courts with territorial jurisdiction over the suspect.
